title: MCP web_fetch accepts any URL — no scheme or host restriction, enabling SSRF to link-local/loopback/internal addresses
why: z.string().url() accepts http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/, http://localhost:9200/_cat/indices, http://10.0.0.5/admin. fetchAndExtract() (src/fetch/fetcher.ts:96) performs the request with no allowlist, no private-IP/DNS-rebind check and no scheme check, and returns the extracted body to the LLM caller. An MCP server is reachable by any prompt-injected content the agent reads, so this is a full read-SSRF primitive into whatever network the server runs on (cloud metadata credentials, internal admin UIs). robots.txt (the only gate) is fetched from the same internal host and fails open (src/fetch/robots.ts:100).

title: Manual redirect following in bpm-pull re-fetches the Location header with no scheme or host validation
code: if (loc) return get(new URL(loc, url).href, redirects - 1);
why: get() sets redirect:"manual" then recurses into the raw Location value resolved against the current URL. Nothing checks that the target is still http(s), still public, or still the originally-approved host, and this path never consults robots.txt at all. A public page that 302s to http://169.254.169.254/ or http://127.0.0.1:8080/ is followed and its body returned as markdown. This is a distinct sink from mcp.ts:300 — any allowlist placed on the tool input is bypassed by a redirect, so it must be validated here too.

title: Playwright fetcher buffers the entire response into memory with no size cap
why: res.text() reads an unbounded body; the string is then held in memory, handed to jsdom (which multiplies it several times over as a DOM), and written to disk pretty-printed by cache.write(). A single hostile or merely large URL (a multi-GB HTML/streamed response) exhausts heap and kills the long-lived MCP server. The sibling fetch path proves the author knew the control was needed: src/bpm-pull.ts:16 defines MAX_BYTES = 5MB and enforces it both by Content-Length and while streaming. This path has neither.

title: robots.txt fetch failure is swallowed and the resulting empty allow-everything ruleset is cached for an hour
why: Any error — timeout, DNS failure, TLS error, 5xx, an http-only host (the fetch is hardcoded to https://) — leaves `rules` as the empty default, which isAllowed() treats as "everything permitted". Worse, line 102 then caches that fabricated permissive ruleset under the host for CACHE_TTL_MS (1h), so one transient blip disables robots enforcement for that site for the rest of the hour. The MCP tool description advertises "robots.txt respected" (src/mcp.ts:116). Failing open silently is a policy decision that should at minimum be logged and not cached.

title: robots.txt is evaluated for the requested URL only; redirects are followed without re-checking the final host or path
why: canFetch(url) runs at line 85 against the pre-redirect URL, then the request is issued with redirect:"follow". The response may come from a completely different host and path whose robots.txt disallows it, and that content is extracted, cached and returned. The per-host rate limiter has the same hole — waitForHost() paced the original host, not the one actually hit. Any site can therefore be crawled through an open redirect on a permissive domain, while the tool description claims robots compliance.

title: Chromium is launched with site isolation and origin isolation disabled while loading untrusted third-party pages
why: --disable-features=IsolateOrigins,site-per-process removes the process boundary between origins in a *persistent* profile that accumulates cookies and site data across runs, and which is then pointed at arbitrary attacker-chosen search-result pages. That is exactly the configuration site isolation exists to protect (Spectre-class cross-origin reads, compromised-renderer cross-site data access). The flag is present only as anti-bot-detection cargo cult; it is not needed for the stealth goals that the other flags serve.

title: bpm-pull's fetch has no timeout — a slow-loris server hangs the request forever
why: No AbortSignal is passed, and the streaming read loop below has no clock either, so a server that trickles bytes below MAX_BYTES holds the connection open indefinitely. pullmdSearch fires four of these in parallel via Promise.allSettled and awaits all of them, so one non-responding engine stalls the whole SERP path with no upper bound; in the MCP server this burns the client's request budget with no diagnostic. The sibling fetcher gets this right (src/fetch/fetcher.ts:105 AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs)).

title: A regex is compiled from remote robots.txt content and run against the request path — catastrophic backtracking is remotely controllable
why: pathMatches() turns each rule into a regex by escaping metacharacters but expanding every '*' to '.*'. A rule such as Disallow: /a*a*a*a*a*a*a*a*b compiles to a chain of unbounded wildcards; matched against a long path of 'a's it backtracks polynomially in the number of wildcards (O(n^k)) and pins the event loop. The input is a third-party file fetched over the network, and isAllowed() runs the match once per rule, so a single hostile robots.txt (or a compromised CDN) is a remote DoS on the crawler process. There is no rule-count cap, no length cap and no match timeout.

title: decodeBing/decodeDdg are byte-for-byte copies of src/decoders.ts, which production code never imports
why: src/decoders.ts exports decodeBingRedirect and decodeDdgUddg and is imported by exactly one file: tests/decoders.test.ts. The live search path uses these private copies instead. The tests therefore assert on a module that ships to nobody, while the code that actually decodes every Bing/DDG result URL is untested. This is the worst form of duplication — it converts a real test suite into decoration and guarantees the two copies drift (they already have: see the third copy inlined at src/engines/bing.ts:56).

title: A third copy of the Bing redirect decoder is inlined inside page.evaluate and has already drifted from the other two
why: The same base64url decode logic exists in src/decoders.ts, in src/engines/http-configs.ts:16, and again here — this copy using atob() instead of Buffer.from(...,'base64'), which throws on characters the Node version tolerates and yields latin1 (mojibake) for any non-ASCII byte rather than UTF-8. Three implementations of one 6-line transform means a fix to the Bing URL format must be found and applied in three places; historically it will be applied to one.

title: The Google (and Brave) result parser exists twice — browser copy and jsdom copy — and the two selector lists have already diverged
why: src/engines/google.ts:45-95 and src/engines/http-configs.ts:162-205 are the same ~40-line parser pasted twice. This snippet selector is present in the browser copy and missing from the HTTP copy, so identical markup yields a snippet on one path and an empty string on the other — an invisible quality regression depending on which path happened to win. The parse body is pure DOM API and runs unmodified in jsdom; it should be one exported function used by both, exactly as the config object already does for buildUrl/detectBlocked.

title: Ternary whose two branches are identical — end-of-path anchoring ($) is written but never implemented
why: Both arms produce `^${escaped}`, so the condition rule.endsWith("$") decides nothing. It also cannot work as intended: '$' is inside the escape character class on line 49, so a rule like Disallow: /private$ is compiled with a literal '\$' and matches only paths that really contain a dollar sign. The result is that every $-anchored robots rule silently stops matching — the crawler ignores exclusions the site owner wrote. A branch that computes the same value on both sides is a hallmark of generated code that was never executed.

title: --debug is documented, parsed, and threaded through three layers, but no engine ever reads it
why: debug is declared in SearchOptions (src/types.ts:17), defaulted in searchAll (src/index.ts:52), forced into the adapter contract via Required<Omit<...>> and passed to every adapter.search call — yet grep finds zero reads inside src/engines/*. The help text's promise ("Keep the browser visible") is doubly false: visibility is controlled by --headless, and nothing changes when --debug is set. A user debugging a failing engine gets no extra output whatsoever.

title: origAttachShadow is captured and never used in the iframe-patching block
why: The variable is read from Element.prototype and then dropped; only origCreateElement on the next line is actually used. Either the shadow-DOM leg of the anti-detection patch was planned and never written (in which case shadow-root iframes still expose navigator.webdriver and the stealth claim is partly false), or it is pure noise. Both readings are defects, and a linter would have caught it — evidence nothing lints this file.

title: MCP server advertises the pre-rename product name and a version unrelated to the package
code: const server = new McpServer({ name: "playwright-search", version: "0.1.0" });
why: package.json is @bpmforge/quarry at 0.4.0; the server announces itself to every client as name "playwright-search", version "0.1.0". Clients key tool namespaces, logs and telemetry off this handshake, so bug reports and cache/config keys will name a product that no longer exists at a version that never shipped. The same stale identity is baked into the on-disk cache path ~/.playwright-search/cache (src/fetch/cache.ts:33), the browser profile dir (src/browser.ts:18) and the CLI banner (src/cli.ts:82); the version string is the one that actually crosses a wire.

title: Startpage block regex uses \Z, a Python end-of-string anchor that JavaScript reads as a literal 'Z'
why: JavaScript has no \Z escape; in a RegExp it degrades to the character Z. The lookahead therefore terminates a result block at the next '[]('-anchor OR at the first capital Z anywhere in the text — so any Startpage result whose snippet contains a word starting with Z (or an acronym, or 'Zero-trust') is silently truncated, and the final block ends at the first Z instead of end-of-input. The idiom is a direct paste from a Python implementation, unverified against the language it now runs in.

title: A regex-based main-content extractor is hand-rolled while @mozilla/readability is already a production dependency in the same codebase
why:
@mozilla/readability + jsdom are declared dependencies and are used correctly 40 lines away in src/extract/readability.ts. This reimplementation parses HTML with /<(article|main|section|div)...>([\s\S]*?)<\/\1>/ — a non-greedy regex that cannot handle nesting, so any wrapper
matches only up to the FIRST closing
and its density score is computed over a truncated fragment; the outermost real article container is systematically mis-scored. The result is that the two fetch paths in this product apply different, incompatible notions of "main content", and the worse one is the default for the pullmd tools. The header comment ("our own readability heuristic, no libraries") states the intent explicitly, which is what makes it a decision rather than an accident.

title: web_search dedupe is O(n^2) with a full URL re-parse per comparison, next to an unused Set that already answers the question
why: For every incoming result this linear-scans `merged` and calls normalizeUrl (a WHATWG URL parse, searchParams mutation, toString and toLowerCase) on each element already in the list. With 4 engines x top 20 that is ~80 results and thousands of redundant URL parses per call. The `seen` Set two lines below already holds exactly the normalized keys, and pipeline.ts:35 solves the same problem correctly with a Map<key, entry>. The parsed keys should be stored once, giving O(n).

title: BM25 scoring compiles a fresh RegExp for every (paragraph x query term) pair inside the hot loop
why: The regex depends only on `term`, yet it is constructed inside paragraphs.map, so an article of 300 paragraphs with 8 query terms compiles 2400 identical regexes per source — and web_research runs this per source per call. Compiling the escaped patterns once, before the map, is a two-line change. This is the innermost loop of the only CPU-bound work the product does.

title: detectPaywall lowercases the entire raw HTML document twice per hint inside a loop
why: fullHtml.toLowerCase() allocates a complete copy of the document — routinely 0.5-5 MB — and it is called twice per iteration over five hints, so up to ten full-document copies per extracted page, all identical. Combined with the seven whole-document regex tests above it, paywall detection can cost more than the Readability parse it follows. Hoisting one `const lower = fullHtml.toLowerCase()` removes nine allocations.

title: Cache writes use blocking sync I/O — and JSON.stringify with 2-space pretty-printing — on the async fetch path
why: writeFileSync (plus mkdirSync and readFileSync on the read side) halts the event loop while serializing the full raw HTML of every fetched page. searchAndFetch runs a concurrency pool of 3-4 fetches, so each completion blocks all peers, the MCP stdio transport and progress notifications. The `null, 2` argument inflates a multi-megabyte machine-only artifact for no reader. fs/promises with unpretty JSON is a drop-in fix.

title: The Promise.race timeout timer is never cleared, keeping the event loop alive after the work is done
why: setTimeout's handle is discarded, so when an engine returns quickly the timer still holds a ref on the loop for the remaining timeoutMs (default 20s, one per engine). The CLI therefore sits idle after printing results instead of exiting, and the long-lived MCP process accumulates a pending timer per engine per call. Capturing the id and clearing it in a finally (or .unref()) fixes it. The losing adapter promise is also left running unobserved, so a browser context can still be opening after the run is reported complete.

title: With the default ua='*', every User-agent block is treated as ours, merging unrelated bots' rules into one ruleset
why: `ourUa === "*"` makes `active` true for every User-agent line in the file, so uaRules accumulates the disallow list of GPTBot, AhrefsBot, and any other agent the site names — and because uaRules is then non-empty, line 41 returns it in preference to the genuine '*' block. A site that blocks one aggressive crawler while permitting '*' causes this crawler to refuse URLs it is explicitly allowed to fetch, and conversely a site whose '*' block is restrictive but whose named blocks are permissive is under-restricted. The intended semantics ('*' means "use the star block") is what starRules already implements; the union is a logic error.

title: serpWithFallback calls searchAll without headless, so the stdio MCP server launches a visible Chromium window
code: const runs = await searchAll(query, { engines: [...ENGINES] as EngineId[] });
why: searchAll defaults headless to false (src/index.ts:53). Every other handler in this file threads an explicit headless flag (default true) into the search; this one omits it. On the fallback path — which is the normal path whenever plain fetch is blocked — a browser window pops onto the user's desktop, and on a headless host with no display the launch fails outright, turning a degraded result into a hard error. Sibling entry points into the same function disagree about the same option.

title: `{} as FetchResult` asserts a fully-populated result object where none exists
why: Every consumer is told by the type system that `fetched` has url/status/contentType/fetch/extract, but between dedupe() and the pool assignment it is an empty object. Any early return, exception, or future code path that reads a result before enrichment gets undefined where the type promises a string — and because the assertion silences the compiler, that bug surfaces only at runtime. The honest type is `fetched?: FetchResult` or a two-stage type (DedupedResult -> EnrichedResult); the cast exists purely to skip that modelling.

title: Cache files are JSON.parse'd and cast to CacheEntry with no schema validation, so one corrupt file can crash a whole request
why: The try/catch covers only parse and the expiry read. A file that parses as valid JSON but lacks `fetch` (truncated write after a crash — writes are non-atomic, see write() at line 67) returns an object whose shape violates the type; the caller then dereferences cached.fetch.finalUrl at src/fetch/fetcher.ts:65, OUTSIDE any try, throwing a TypeError that rejects the pool worker and fails the entire searchAndFetch call. zod is already a dependency and is used for MCP input; validating here (or writing via a temp file + rename) turns a hard failure into a cache miss.

title: Numeric CLI flags are parseInt'd with no NaN or range check, producing a crash or an unbounded run
why: --concurrency abc yields NaN, which reaches new Array(Math.min(NaN, len)) in pipeline.pool and throws RangeError: Invalid array length with no useful message. --top abc yields NaN, and every extractor guards with `if (out.length >= max) break` — a comparison that is always false for NaN — so the result cap silently disappears. Negative values are equally unchecked and hit the same RangeError. One Number.isInteger + range check per flag.

title: Comma-split CLI input is cast straight to EngineId[] with no membership check
why: `as EngineId[]` tells the compiler the strings are valid engine ids; nothing verifies it. `--engines ddgg` produces `ALL[id] === undefined` at src/index.ts:59 and the adapter.search call throws "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'search')", which searchAll's catch converts into an EngineRun error string — so a typo is reported as an engine failure rather than a usage error, and with --json the user sees a per-engine internal TypeError. The valid set is a four-element literal union; filtering against it is one line.

title: Three copies of normalizeUrl exist and one strips a parameter the others keep, so the dedupe key differs by code path
why: src/pipeline.ts:66, src/mcp.ts:526 and src/pullmd-serp.ts:409 are the same function, except this copy also deletes the "ref" query parameter. The same two URLs therefore merge in searchAndFetch but stay separate in web_search and pullmdSearch, producing duplicate "sources" in one tool and not another for reasons no reader can discover without diffing three files. All three also lowercase the whole URL including the path, which wrongly merges case-sensitive paths (/API vs /api) on any non-Windows origin. One exported helper.

title: Every parsed SERP document is given the base URL https://example.com/, corrupting relative result links and neutering the guard against them
code: return new JSDOM(html, { virtualConsole: vc, url: "https://example.com/" })
why: makeDoc() hardcodes the document URL, so anchor.href resolves relative hrefs against example.com. The Brave and Google HTTP configs read a.href directly (src/engines/http-configs.ts:145 and :178), so any relative result link is emitted as https://example.com/... and later fetched. The very filter meant to catch this — a.href.startsWith("/search") at http-configs.ts:179 — is dead code, because .href is always absolute in jsdom; the sibling check a.href.includes("google.com/search") also stops matching once the base is example.com. The real request URL is available at the call site and should be passed in.

title: Per-host rate limiting reads the timestamp, sleeps, then writes it — concurrent callers all sleep the same interval and fire together
why: The map is only updated after the await, so N concurrent fetches to one host read the same `prev`, compute the same gap and wake simultaneously — the enforced spacing is 1.2-2.5s between BATCHES, not between requests. searchAndFetch runs a pool of concurrency 3-4 over deduped results that frequently share a host (docs sites, Stack Overflow, GitHub), so the politeness guarantee the MCP tool advertises ("rate-limited per-domain") does not hold precisely when it matters. The fix is to reserve the next slot synchronously before awaiting.

title: bpm-pull's paceFor has the same read-sleep-write race, and its `now` parameter is ignored on the write side
why: Second, independent implementation of the same broken pattern: the timestamp is written only after the sleep, so the parallel Promise.allSettled fan-out in pullmdSearch and the parallel candidate fetches in web_research_pullmd never observe each other's reservations. The declared HOST_PACE_MS entry for www.reddit.com (12s) is therefore not enforced across concurrent reads of two Reddit URLs — exactly the case it was written for. Note also the injectable `now` used for the elapsed computation is discarded here in favour of Date.now(), so the function is not deterministic under test.

title: The regex-escaping character class is double-escaped and matches nothing, so the escape call is a no-op
why: The class is written [.*+?^${}()|[\\]\\\\] — the class closes after the escaped backslash, and the trailing \\\\] is parsed as two literal backslashes followed by ']', so the pattern only matches a metacharacter followed by '\\]'. Verified: "a.b*c".replace(re, "\\$&") returns "a.b*c" unchanged. Today this is harmless because tokenizeQuery strips everything outside [a-z0-9], but scoreParagraphs is exported and takes arbitrary queryTerms — the first caller that passes a raw term gets an injected or throwing pattern from a guard that looks correct in review. The correct form is used elsewhere in this repo (src/pullmd-serp.ts:284), so the two can be compared directly.

title: searchAndFetch filters out failed engine runs and drops their error text with no log and no return channel
why: searchAll carefully captures per-engine `error` and `durationMs`; this filter throws all of it away. The EnrichedResult[] contract has no field for it, so web_research (src/mcp.ts:173) literally cannot distinguish "3 engines were CAPTCHA-blocked" from "3 engines found nothing" — both render as fewer sources. The asymmetry is inside one file: the sibling web_search handler does surface failures (src/mcp.ts:277-281, "engines that failed: ..."). Captchas, rate-limit bans and selector rot — the failures this product exists to manage — are exactly what is silenced on its primary path.

title: The fast HTTP search path's failure is swallowed by a bare catch before falling back to a full browser launch
why: The thrown Error carries the actual diagnosis — HTTP status, "captcha challenge", "0 results parsed" (meaning the selectors rotted) — and it is discarded without a single stderr line. The consequence is a silent 30x latency and memory cliff (a Chromium launch) that operators cannot attribute, and permanent selector rot that never surfaces because the browser path masks it. The brave and google adapters at least inspect the message before discarding it (src/engines/brave.ts:103-110); this one and ddg.ts:128 do not, so sibling adapters have three different error-handling contracts.

title: A host is permanently blacklisted for the process lifetime after 3 failures, with no log, no expiry and no way to observe or reset it
why: This is the most consequential state transition in the fetch layer — after it, every URL on that host returns skipped:"blacklisted" with status 0 — and it emits nothing. In a long-lived MCP server three transient 503s permanently blind the agent to a documentation domain for the rest of the process, and the operator sees only "[skipped: blacklisted]" with no record of when or why it happened. Neither the counter nor the set is bounded or aged; resetForTests() is the only way out and it is test-only.

title: Corrupt or unreadable cache entries are silently reported as a cache miss forever
why: A truncated or permission-denied cache file returns null, so the URL is refetched on every single call and the bad file is never repaired or removed — a permanent silent performance regression with no signal. It also hides the real bug it would otherwise expose: write() is non-atomic (writeFileSync straight onto the destination path), so an interrupted run leaves exactly these half-written files. Distinguishing ENOENT (normal) from a parse or IO error (abnormal, log it and unlink) costs three lines.
